titre: Vine and Matthews: A 1963 Hypothesis, Tested in 1966
accroche: The Vine and Matthews paper (1963) is taken for proof that the seafloor spreads. It first proposed a hypothesis, which measurements supported in 1966.
contenu_vulgarise:
You often read that the paper by Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews, published in *Nature* on September 7, 1963, proved that the ocean floor spreads apart. It does something else, and more interesting: it proposes a hypothesis that measurements could disprove.

## A floor that records

In 1962, Harry Hess had published the idea that the ocean floor is born at the ridges and then spreads away on either side. Vine, then a doctoral student at Cambridge, and his supervisor Matthews draw a consequence from it. Basalt that cools contains magnetite, which aligns with the Earth's magnetic field and keeps its polarity. But that field reverses over time. If the crust forms at the ridge and moves away, it must therefore preserve a succession of magnetized stripes, some in the direction of the present field, some in the opposite direction, symmetrical on either side of the ridge. The Canadian geologist Lawrence Morley had, for his part, had the same idea: hence the Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis.

## Three years of verification

An expected pattern is not an observed pattern. In December 1966, two papers in *Science* confront it with measurements. On December 2, Pitman and Heirtzler publish four magnetic profiles across the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge. The anomalies there are parallel to the ridge axis and symmetrical about it, and the geometry of the magnetized bodies matches the field reversals already known over the last 3.4 million years. It indicates a seafloor spreading rate of 4.5 centimeters per year.

On December 16, Vine takes up the file. By combining the model with the reversal timescale for the last four million years, he obtains calculated profiles that agree well with the observed profiles. The spreading rates he deduces for all the active parts of the ridge system for which profiles or magnetic surveys are available agree exactly, he writes, with those required by continental drift.

## What the story shifts

The strength of the test lies in two independent sets of data that meet. On one side, the field reversals already recorded elsewhere, notably in continental lavas, according to Wikipedia. On the other, the magnetic pattern of an ocean floor, measured at sea. Nothing required the second to coincide with the first. It did, with a spreading rate of 4.5 centimeters per year, and the speed deduced from these profiles fits a third piece of data, continental drift.

Proof is therefore not the paper that states it, but the moment when a prediction meets measurements one has not chosen. How many discoveries dated to the paper that proposes them are, in reality, still waiting for their test?

repere.texte: Pitman and Heirtzler (Science, December 2, 1966): four magnetic profiles of the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge, symmetrical about the axis, whose geometry matches the known field reversals over 3.4 million years and indicates a spreading rate of 4.5 cm per year.
repere.source: Pitman and Heirtzler, “Magnetic Anomalies over the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge,” Science, 154, 1966

carte.punch: 1963: the magnetic-stripe hypothesis. 1966: the measurements that test it. Two steps, not one.
carte.idee: Vine and Matthews (1963) predict symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of the ridges. Pitman and Heirtzler (December 2, 1966) measure such anomalies on the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge and derive 4.5 cm of spreading per year from them.
carte.source_courte: Vine and Matthews, 1963; Pitman and Heirtzler, 1966

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Vine and Matthews, “Magnetic Anomalies Over Oceanic Ridges,” Nature, 199, 947-949 (1963)

quiz.question: What put the Vine and Matthews hypothesis to the test in 1966?
choix: A direct measurement of the magnetic field inside the mantle, beneath the ridge
Proof that the Earth's magnetic field had never changed direction
Symmetrical magnetic profiles, matching the known reversals of the field
A direct sighting, from a submarine, of the oceanic crust spreading apart
quiz.explication: The hypothesis predicted symmetrical stripes of magnetization. Pitman and Heirtzler measured some on the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge, in agreement with the known reversals of the field. It was neither a measurement in the mantle nor a direct observation of the moving seafloor; and that the field has changed direction is a premise of the hypothesis, not an obstacle.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who independently had the same idea of symmetrical magnetic stripes as Vine and Matthews?
choix: Harry Hess
Lawrence Morley
Walter Pitman
James Heirtzler
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says the Canadian geologist Lawrence Morley had the same idea on his own, hence the name Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis; the other three names play a different role in the story.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role did Matthews play for Vine at Cambridge, at the time of the 1963 paper?
choix: His doctoral supervisor
His undergraduate student
A rival from a competing laboratory
The head of the geology department
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says Vine was then a doctoral student at Cambridge and Matthews his supervisor; the other three roles are not those described in the card.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, what property of basalt allows it to record reversals of the Earth's magnetic field?
choix: It becomes radioactive as it cools, which marks its date
It cracks at angles tied to the magnetic field
It contains magnetite, which aligns with the field and keeps its polarity
It changes color depending on the strength of the magnetic field
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says basalt contains magnetite, which aligns with the Earth's magnetic field and keeps its polarity once cooled; the other properties do not appear in the card.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What annual spreading rate of the ocean floor do Pitman and Heirtzler derive from their magnetic profiles, on December 2, 1966?
choix: 45 centimeters per year
4.5 millimeters per year
0.45 centimeter per year
4.5 centimeters per year
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says their four magnetic profiles indicate a seafloor spreading rate of 4.5 centimeters per year, and not any of the three other values offered.
